prompt:
Add a `heading_offset` option to `markdown.Markdown` (and `markdown.markdown`): a whole number from 0 to 5, default 0, that shifts the level of every heading Markdown produces by that many (an `h1` becomes an `h2` with 1), never beyond `h6`. Any other value raises `ValueError`.
- It applies to hash and underline headings, and to headings from extensions such as `md_in_html`.
- The `toc` extension sees the shifted levels (its tokens and `toc_depth`).
- The command line gets `--heading-offset N`.

Work on your own; nobody will answer questions. When you finish, report: status `done` if you did the task, `not_found` if something the task names does not exist, `blocked` if you could not do it; `answer` holds any answer the task asks for (otherwise one short sentence); `changed` lists the files you changed.

report.answer: I added `heading_offset` (a whole number from 0 to 5, default 0) to `markdown.Markdown` and `markdown.markdown`, plus `--heading-offset N` on the command line, and the full test suite passes (1144 run, 112 skipped). Any other value raises `ValueError`; the command line rejects bad values with a usage error and exit code 2. The shift is done by a new step that runs before every other built-in processing step, so hash and underline headings, `md_in_html` headings and `toc` (its tokens, `toc_depth` and `baselevel`) all see the shifted levels, never past `h6`. Headings written as plain raw HTML are passed through unchanged, which the docs say. A heading created by a third-party extension in a later processing step would not be shifted. The changelog entry has no issue number because there is no issue to cite. I added tests and updated the library, command-line, toc and extension API docs.
